facts.raw_span: A man in his 60s presented with a 10-year history of a slowly progressive, asymptomatic cutaneous eruption on his left leg
16-year history of diabetes mellitus
being treated with metformin
no history of another endocrine disorder or malignant neoplasm
no family history of similar cutaneous findings
Reddish brown hyperkeratotic papules 1 to 10 mm wide were present on the front and back of the left leg from knee to ankle
Removal of the scales caused slight bleeding
The rest of the physical examination findings were unremarkable
Hematological and biochemical test results were unremarkable
Lesional skin biopsy
compact hyperkeratosis, epidermal atrophy, and bandlike lymphocyte infiltrate in the superficial dermis

concepts.why: The patient's 10-year history of a slowly progressive, asymptomatic cutaneous eruption on his left leg, combined with the presence of reddish brown hyperkeratotic papules and the lesional skin biopsy results, are consistent with necrobiosis lipoidica, a condition often associated with diabetes mellitus.
The patient's cutaneous eruption, characterized by reddish brown hyperkeratotic papules, could be consistent with granuloma annulare, a condition that can present with similar skin lesions.
The patient's cutaneous eruption, located on the lower leg, could be consistent with stasis dermatitis, a condition that can cause similar skin changes due to poor circulation.

The patient's 16-year history of diabetes mellitus, combined with the presence of cutaneous eruption, could be consistent with diabetic dermopathy, a condition that can cause skin changes in patients with diabetes.
The patient's cutaneous eruption, characterized by reddish brown hyperkeratotic papules, could be consistent with psoriasis, a condition that can present with similar skin lesions.
The patient's cutaneous eruption, characterized by reddish brown hyperkeratotic papules, could be consistent with lichen planus, a condition that can present with similar skin lesions.

The patient's cutaneous eruption, combined with the presence of bandlike lymphocyte infiltrate in the superficial dermis, could be consistent with scleroderma, a condition that can cause skin changes and inflammation.

The patient's cutaneous eruption, combined with the presence of bandlike lymphocyte infiltrate in the superficial dermis, could be consistent with lupus erythematosus, a condition that can cause skin changes and inflammation.
